title: The king who looked too long
hook: a king in heaven stares too long at the river goddess, and gods under a curse ask her for a terrible favor
carry: karma carries into the next birth
tomorrow: a woman rises from a river. whose wife will she be?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Astika asked, the fire stopped, and Janamejaya sat down to hear the story. Listening to the sacred story is itself devotion.
screen: `LISTENING TO THE SACRED STORY IS ITSELF DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: A court in heaven. The gods are gathered before Brahma, and among them is a king, Mahabhisha, who earned his place there by his deeds on earth. Then the river goddess Ganga arrives. A wind lifts her garment. The gods lower their eyes. Mahabhisha doesn't. He looks, and keeps looking. Brahma sees it, and tells him: you will be born again among mortals. This part of the Kuru story starts with a stare.
screen: `A COURT IN HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS LOWER THEIR EYES.` → `ONE KING KEEPS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: The text sets it up with two curses, side by side. The first is Mahabhisha's. Brahma sends him down to be born on earth, and tells him that Ganga, the one who stole his mind, will cross him there, and that his time on earth will end when he finally loses his temper with her. Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of a good king named Pratipa. The second curse belongs to the Vasus, a group of gods. On her way back, Ganga meets them, downcast. The sage Vasishtha has cursed them to be born as men, and they don't want to linger in human lives. So they ask a strange favor: be our mother on earth, and as each of us is born, throw us into your waters, so we're set free at once. Ganga agrees, with one condition: one son has to live. Each Vasu gives a portion of his power to that son, who will live long and, they say, have no children. Hold that detail. Now look at what this story takes for granted, because Hindus do too. A king can earn heaven by his deeds and still be born again. Gods can be born as men. This is samsara, the round of births, and karma is what turns it: what you do, even where you let your eyes rest, carries into the next birth. Even heaven isn't the end. That's why the Vasus don't ask for long lives; they ask for release. Hindus call that release moksha, and we'll watch Ganga give it.
screen: `MAHABHISHA: BORN AGAIN ON EARTH.` · `THE VASUS: CURSED BY VASISHTHA.` · `THROW US INTO YOUR WATERS.` · `SAMSARA: THE ROUND OF BIRTHS.` · then, large: `KARMA CARRIES INTO THE NEXT BIRTH.`

segments.voice: A river keeps moving; it doesn't hold on, so let the breath do the same for a few rounds, eyes lowered or closed. Notice where your attention wants to go: a screen, a worry, a face, a plan. In this story even a look leaves a mark. Each time your attention pulls, let it come back down to the breath, the way the gods in Brahma's court lowered their eyes.
Mahabhisha. The king whose stare wouldn't lower in heaven, sent to be born on earth, where Ganga, bound by a promise to the Vasus, waits to cross him.
Take this with you: karma carries into the next birth. Tomorrow: a woman rises from a river. whose wife will she be? That's day seven hundred four.

screen: `DAY 704 COUNTS.` → `THE MAHABHARATA · 8 OF 182.` → `TOMORROW: A WOMAN RISES FROM A RIVER. WHOSE WIFE WILL SHE BE?`

howItsDone: At the Ganga, the river is honored as a goddess: pilgrims bathe in her waters, some carry Ganga water home in sealed vessels, and lamps are offered to her at evening aarti on her banks.

fork.setup: a friend says reincarnation means you come back as yourself, memories and all, for another try. by today's story, what's closer to the Hindu idea?
options: the self is born again into a new life shaped by its karma: Mahabhisha becomes Shantanu.
only bad people are reborn; good people stay in heaven forever.
rebirth is only for gods, like the Vasus.
fork.reveal: Mahabhisha had earned heaven and was still born again, as Shantanu. in Hindu teaching, heaven is a stop, not the end; release from rebirth is moksha.

original.note: Sanskrit Gaṅgā, the river and the goddess: in this story, the mother of the Vasus on earth.

chat.says: Nani's story tonight: a king in heaven gets sent back down for STARING. Sam asked 'wait, do Hindus actually believe in reincarnation?' i said 'kinda?' lol. help
options: many do: samsara. we're born again by our karma, like Mahabhisha, a king in heaven sent back for one stare.
only as a metaphor; nobody takes it literally.
yes, but only bad people get reborn. good people stay in heaven forever.
chat.meaning: Mahabhisha earned heaven and was still born again for one stare. Many Hindus believe in samsara: rebirth shaped by karma, until release, moksha.

Brahma.meaning: the creator god, before whom the gods gather

Ganga.meaning: the sacred river, and the goddess of the river

Vasus.meaning: a group of gods, cursed to be born as men

Vasishtha.meaning: the sage who cursed the Vasus

samsara.meaning: the round of birth, death and rebirth

moksha.meaning: release from the round of rebirth

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Mahabhisha in Brahma's court; Ganga and the Vasus)

notes: All paraphrase. Check Brahma's words to Mahabhisha: that Ganga will do things displeasing to him on earth and that he will return when his anger is roused; the script says his time on earth ends 'when he finally loses his temper with her'.
Check the Vasus' bargain: Ganga's condition that one son live, each Vasu giving a portion (an eighth in the text) of his energy, and the surviving son having no offspring.
Mahabhisha 'chooses' Pratipa as his father; confirm.
howItsDone describes common Ganga practices (bathing, carrying water, evening aarti); confirm phrasing.
